YOGA-2018JUL-P2-Q89.question_text: Which of the following is not a kind of pranayama?
YOGA-2018JUL-P2-Q89.passage:
Maharshi Patanjali has described eight limbs of yoga for attaining kaivalya. These limbs are: yama (universal moral commandments), niyama (self-purification through discipline), asana, pranayama (rhythmic control of prana), pratyahara (withdrawal and complete mastery of the senses), dharana, dhyana and samadhi (the state of supreme consciousness). Of these, the first five are considered bahiranga (outer) yoga and the remaining three antaranga (inner) yoga. The yamas are moral rules for society and the individual: ahimsa, satya, asteya, brahmacharya and aparigraha. The niyamas are codes of conduct that apply to personal discipline. The five niyamas are shaucha, santosha, tapa, svadhyaya and Ishvara pranidhana.

The third limb of ashtanga yoga is asana. The practice of asana brings steadiness and ease, and the person is not easily affected by the pairs of opposites such as heat and cold, thirst and hunger, attraction and aversion. Pranayama means the expansion or regulation of the breath, or of the life force. It is of four kinds: bahya vritti, abhyantara vritti, stambha vritti and bahyabhyantara vishayakshepi. Pranayama should be practised only after mastery of asana. Pranayama removes the covering over the light of knowledge and makes the mind fit for dharana. Pratyahara is the practice of withdrawing the senses, mind and consciousness from contact with external objects and drawing them inwards towards the self. Pratyahara culminates in complete control over the organs of knowledge. Dharana means fixing attention on a chosen point or area inside or outside the body. Dhyana is keeping the chitta continuously focused on that one point or area. Samadhi is the state of supreme consciousness, where the sense of self is lost. Ashtanga yoga is the best path to attaining kaivalya.

YOGA-2018JUL-P2-Q95.question_text: When was the second International Day of Yoga celebrated?
YOGA-2018JUL-P2-Q95.passage:
On 27 September 2014, addressing the 69th session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), India's Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi called on the world community to celebrate a day as 'International Day of Yoga'. On 11 December 2014, the 193 members of the UN General Assembly, with a record 177 co-sponsoring countries, unanimously approved the resolution to celebrate 21 June as 'International Day of Yoga'. Yoga practice brings about the unity of mind and body, thought and action, restraint and fulfilment, and harmony between human beings and nature. It is a holistic approach to health and well-being. Yoga is known for promoting health, preventing disease and managing various lifestyle-related illnesses. The 'Common Yoga Protocol' was prepared to spread knowledge of the methods and benefits of yoga practice among the world's population.

The Ministry of AYUSH successfully organised the first International Day of Yoga at Rajpath, New Delhi, on 21 June 2015. Two Guinness World Records were set at the event: the largest yoga session, with 35,985 participants, and the participation of citizens of the most nations (84) in a single yoga session. The second International Day of Yoga was held on 21 June 2016 at the Capitol Complex, Chandigarh, where more than 30,000 people joined our Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi. For the first time, 150 persons with disabilities performed the Common Yoga Protocol at the International Day of Yoga celebration at the Capitol Complex, Chandigarh. A two-day international conference on "Yoga for Body and Beyond" was held at Vigyan Bhawan, New Delhi, on 21 and 22 June 2016. Shri Narendra Modi celebrated the third International Day of Yoga in Lucknow on 21 June 2017.
